articles.title: ELI STEELE: The terror of being called racist is crushing free speech in America
articles.summary: Shelby Steele's son, filmmaker Eli Steele, explores how the terror of being called racist silenced a generation and fueled the diversity industry's unchecked power.
articles.body: When my father, Shelby Steele, author, columnist and senior fellow at Stanford University's Hoover Institution, began publishing his essays on race in the late 1980s, my teenage self was often by his side when he gave speeches. After each speech, the same scene unfolded as a crowd of people gathered to the side of the podium, each wanting a word. I remember one man in particular who hurried to reach my father first. He wore a corduroy sports coat with leather elbow patches. He said, "Dr. Steele, that was truly a remarkable speech. I want to thank you for saying the things you said up there." My father thanked him, and the man lowered his voice and leaned in as if to share a conspiracy. "You know I can't say those things." My father leaned back and said, "Why not?" The man smiled, as if to say, come on, "I am a White man." 15-YEAR-OLD BLACK TEEN'S MURDER REVEALS THE UGLY TRUTH ABOUT WHITE GUILT IN AMERICA My father had spent the past hour arguing for moving beyond the stifling limits of racial identity to the far greater possibilities within the American identity. The man agreed with every word, yet he could not bring himself to say them. He did not do so out of modesty but out of fear. To escape the charge of racism, he reduced himself to his race. The fear had done to him exactly what racism does. So, he stayed silent and let others like my father speak for him. No charge in American life carries more destructive power than the accusation of racism. Once charged with this modern-day Scarlet Letter, how do you disprove it? Do you trot out your Black friends and have them testify to your innocence? Or do you look into your accuser’s eyes and say the words that no one believes: I am not a racist? You cannot disprove it — the accusation is the verdict. This terror has reigned since the civil rights era, when the nation admitted to centuries of racial horror and rightfully vowed never to repeat it. Americans wanted to be better. DESCENDANT OF SLAVES SHAMES SMITHSONIAN’S WOKE ‘INDOCTRINATION’ AGAINST THE ‘GREATEST NATION ON EARTH’ For many, this terror came to overtake even the biblical sins. A man could be forgiven for greed, a lie, or even adultery, but not racism. Those sins of the Bible had a way back through confession, repentance and forgiveness. Racism had none. There was no amount of confession that absolved it. There was only endless penance. This terror has reigned since the civil rights era, when the nation admitted to centuries of racial horror and rightfully vowed never to repeat it. Americans wanted to be better. Some Americans went further. They believed that their nation's founding principles were stained with racism to the point that they no longer held any legitimacy or role in their redemptive efforts. They embraced the Marxism of liberation ideology, dividing us into White oppressors and oppressed people of color. And when they came to understand the full power of this White guilt terror, they molded it to their advantage. Anyone who stood in their way also stood in the path of justice. The charge was racism if you were White. It was race traitor if you were Black. GEORGIA DISTRICT QUIETLY TRAINED TEACHERS TO BLAME 'WHITENESS,' 'DECOLONIZE' UNDER FEDERAL CRACKDOWN: REPORT At first, this terror enforced our behavior from the outside, and then it began to seep into our minds. On the nightly news, in newspaper headlines, or before our own eyes — we saw people or companies shamed as racist for not being diverse enough, for a word taken out of context, or for a donation to the wrong cause. Careers ended. Offenders were socially ostracized. We saw all of this, and we began to police our own speech and thoughts out of fear of saying the wrong thing. We even learned how to apologetically preface anything we said that could be misconstrued. We told ourselves we were being decent. We were afraid. SMITHSONIAN PUSHED ‘REVOLTING’ SOCIAL ACTION TRAINING AFTER ‘WHITENESS’ CHART APOLOGY: EXPERT My father defines this terror as White guilt. I have heard many Whites declare, "I have no White guilt." Of course, they don't. One cannot feel actual guilt for what one has not done. White guilt is the collective guilt imposed on the White race for the sins of America's past. It is the terror of being seen as carrying on that racist legacy. Real guilt ends. You make amends, and you are free. White guilt never ends, because there is nothing to atone for, only the burden of skin color to answer for. 1619 PROJECT CREATOR CLAIMS PAYING REPARATIONS WOULD BE ADMISSION THAT US EXISTENCE IS A 'CRIME' The history this terror rests on is real. My own family has ancestors who were born as the property of White men. They worked their entire lives without pay, and their lives held such little value that they could be beaten or even killed. This terror of White guilt has grown into the evil of our time. Far too many of us have surrendered to it out of convenience, and our institutions have grown weaker, our free speech has been constrained, and our children have become less educated. Even Christianity was distorted to support the idea that a White man had more value than a Black man. When the convulsions of the 1960s destroyed the moral legitimacy of the racial order of White supremacy, Whites suddenly found their lie of racial supremacy exposed, and they were without moral authority. An entire race condemned as guilty needed a way to prove it was innocent. What eventually became known as the diversity industry showed no mercy with this power. It understood that this terror could be monetized. ELI STEELE: BOB WOODSON TAUGHT ME AMERICA’S WOUNDS HEAL ONLY THROUGH TRUTH AND COURAGE It was around 1970 that the word diversity began to gain prominence, and it became the societal measure of innocence. Its logic was unforgiving: the more people of color an institution had, the more innocent it became. Absolution was the point. But absolution is a mirage. No one arrives. Paul Rossi, then a math teacher at Grace Church School in New York City, was relieved of his teaching duties after publicly challenging the school's approach to race and later left the school. Rossi’s troubles began when he questioned his school's conditioning of students to view their whiteness as a perpetual apology. In my documentary, "White Guilt," he describes a training session where the administration segregated the entire school into two racial groups. He was placed in the White room. The facilitator warned that they might feel some White feelings, and Paul asked, "What is a White feeling?" CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The trainings, he came to understand, were designed never to arrive. They endlessly expand what counts as racist and push justice beyond reach, into the future, into the keeping of experts. It was never meant to arrive. Widening the charge was how it sustained and grew its power. Real guilt ends. You make amends, and you are free. White guilt never ends, because there is nothing to atone for, only the burden of skin color to answer for. Each flareup, from Trayvon Martin to Michael Brown, escalated the accusation that America is systemically racist. It reached its height during the summer of George Floyd, when a single video led to the reorganization of America and the West in corporate boardrooms, classrooms and the arts. And still it was not enough. No amount of penance can satisfy an accuser whose power depends on your guilt. The formula only needed a new oppressed group and a new oppressor. It is no wonder this terror has spread beyond race. Other protected classes saw the power to be had and recognized the formula that White guilt had established. The constant in this formula was the White oppressor. The variable was the oppressed, a role any approved minority could take up. Yasser Arafat, the PLO and other Palestinian organizations understood this early, courting Black revolutionaries as early as Arafat’s visit with Eldridge Cleaver and the Black Panthers in Algiers in the 1970s. When the Hamas terror attacks of October 7, 2023, happened in Israel, the decades of groundwork paid off. The White guilt-Black power symbiosis became a White guilt-Palestinian one, and the slaughter of Jews was reframed as resistance before the bodies were counted. This terror of White guilt has grown into the evil of our time. Far too many of us have surrendered to it out of convenience, and our institutions have grown weaker, our free speech has been constrained, and our children have become less educated. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Too often, we ask, "Who let it happen?" as if it were done to us. But too many Whites allowed themselves to be reduced to color in hopes that the charge of racism would pass over their heads. And some activists saw in it an easy source of power, defending racial discrimination in the name of justice. The White guilt terror has grown into a great evil of today because we let it. The man who did it is not hard to find. He felt the fear, saw his Whiteness and chose silence, and he is still there, smiling in a corduroy jacket. He never needed permission to say what he believed. He needed courage. So do we. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM ELI STEELE

articles.title: South Korea considers steps to force North Korea apology for DMZ mine blast
articles.summary: Seoul has urged Pyongyang to remove any other mines planted on the southern side of the military demarcation line.
articles.body:
South Korea is weighing measures to force an apology from North Korea over a recent landmine blast that wounded three soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) between the two countries, a Defence Ministry spokesperson has said.

A joint South Korean-United Nations investigation concluded on Monday that two landmines that exploded last month in the DMZ were planted by North Korean forces about a year ago, prompting Seoul to demand an official apology.

“We are not ruling out any options or prejudging anything when it comes to additional measures,” Defence Ministry spokeswoman Chung Bin-na told reporters on Tuesday when asked if steps were being planned to force an apology from Pyongyang.

Chung did not offer specifics about what actions might be employed.

Seoul has also called on nuclear-armed North Korea to remove any other mines planted on the southern side of the military demarcation line (MDL) that runs through the DMZ, the heavily fortified frontier that has divided the Korean Peninsula since the 1953 Armistice Agreement.

Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the September 21 blast, with Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s leader, slamming the call for an apology as “despicable”.

Chung said Seoul is calling on ⁠Pyongyang to come ⁠to the table to ⁠discuss a misalignment of the MDL. Differing views of the border line are one factor contributing to tension in the area, she said.

The comments come a day after South Korea’s military carried out a mine-clearing operation south of the MDL. It pledged to continue with clearing operations in the area if Pyongyang fails to remove the remaining explosives. The United States-led UN Command (UNC) confirmed the mine placement violated the 1953 agreement.

Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul told the Yonhap news agency on Tuesday that the military’s “decisive” response was “unprecedented in history”.

“All responsibility lies with North Korea,” Kang told reporters, adding that armed forces would “respond decisively” to any actions threatening national security.

The escalation comes as Pyongyang rejected diplomatic overtures from Seoul. Unification Minister Chung Dong-young proposed on October 2 that both sides jointly resurvey the MDL, noting that only about 200 of 1,292 original boundary markers remain intact and that Seoul and the UNC differ on roughly 60 percent of border coordinates.

Kim Yo Jong rejected the proposal as a “wild dream”, declaring Pyongyang would define its sovereign boundary “by the use of force, not by means of negotiation”.

articles.title: HUGH HEWITT: Legacy media left half of America out. Fox News let them in
articles.summary: Rush Limbaugh built talk radio's foundation, and Rupert Murdoch proved the same concept for cable news, reshaping conservative media for decades.
articles.body: Some would date the revolution in American media to June 1, 1980, when, at 6:00 p.m. Eastern time, CNN began broadcasting around-the-clock news. But, while CNN was 24/7/365, it differed only in the volume of televised news it carried, not different from the quality or the lean of legacy network news. Indeed, CNN quickly became a part of legacy news. That is what it is aspired to. That is what it became. Others would point to August 4, 1987, as the beginning of the revolution, the date the Federal Communications Commission repealed the "Fairness Doctrine" by a vote of 4-0 under FCC Chairman Dennis R. Patrick’s leadership. Still others would point to August 1, 1988, when Rush Limbaugh launched his program on ABC Radio Networks and began broadcasting over his then 50 affiliates. "Rush built the mall," I tell most audiences interested in the birth of conservative talk radio. "Mike Gallagher, Larry Elder, Mark Levin … we just have stores inside that mall." RUSH LIMBAUGH’S PATRIOTIC LEGACY RETURNS AHEAD OF AMERICA’S 250TH BIRTHDAY TO TEACH KIDS TRUE HISTORY Rush provided "proof of concept" to AM station owners and a demand signal to all of media that half of America was not just under-served but actually unwelcomed. The market responded. Brian Kilmeade, Guy Benson and many others on the Fox Radio Network are part of the ever-expanding news universe on the center-right. "The good bulk of the press in this country was monolithic — liberal to varying degrees," Fox News founder Rupert Murdoch commented on the 10th anniversary of the launch of Fox News in 2006. This was an echo from what he had said at the actual launch ten years ago: "Frankly, all the others look alike. We will be an alternative." JUAN WILLIAMS: MY WIFE THOUGHT I WAS CRAZY TO JOIN FOX NEWS. I'M GLAD I DID Of course, the success of the network and the brand has been phenomenal. What Rush Limbaugh did for radio, Rupert Murdoch did for cable news: Prove the concept that there was an enormous, unmet demand in consumers of news in America for center, center-right and conservative news. As with Limbaugh, so with Murdoch: Great success followed by others entering the lists with the same basic model. Even a cursory glance at cable news ratings screams out that Murdoch was right and perhaps right far beyond what anyone suspected. Fox News doesn’t merely dominate the ratings, it crushes them. Through three decades of rising to and remaining on top, the formula has been the same: Put professionals on the air who reflect what patriotic and America-loving portions of the news-consuming public believe and ask them to present the news in a fair, measured way through the start of prime time. Always be reasonable. Always be open to other views. Use light humor and sly derision by all means, but even the "opinion hosts" work to "stay within the 20s" even as daytime stays firmly "within the 40s." Counterfactuals are never very productive, so spare yourself the time you would waste imagining a world in which Fox News had not been launched and thrived. It would be — even its worst critics should admit this — so much less interesting, so much more gray than had legacy news been left to its own devices, pumping out the same old, same old over the past 30 years. Having carved out for itself a formidable Gibraltar of a fortress for its brand, it is unlikely that Fox News will be displaced from the top of cable news specifically, and indeed increasingly "the news" generally for years to come. What we see now are the first, tentative steps of legacy media to consciously try and shrug off the reputation for bias it built for itself since the Vietnam War turned legacy media into a vast swamp of advocacy journalism. FOX NEWS MEDIA TOPS YOUTUBE FOR EIGHTH STRAIGHT QUARTER WITH 918 MILLION VIEWS That’s a huge mountain to climb, especially as so many previous attempts have failed. Like universities that hire a visiting professor with glowing credentials on the right for a year or two of appointment as a "Visiting Scholar," the underlying institution is looking for camouflage, not a genuine commitment to the ideas it has long locked out of its halls. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Thirty years down the road, the country will again check in and see that "journalism" remains a craft, not a profession, and the best craftsmen are fully aware of the world around them, not blinkered to half or more of the news horizon.

articles.title: Burger King marketing boss says 'guest does rule' but says one thing can't be forced
articles.summary: A Burger King executive reveals how the fast-food chain wants employees to treat customers like royalty: "The guest does rule," he tells Fox News Digital.
articles.body: Burger King has spent decades telling customers to "Have it Your Way." Now, the Miami-based fast-food chain wants its employees to make sure guests feel like they rule. The philosophy is reflected in Burger King's more recent "You Rule" slogan — and in how the company approaches hospitality inside its restaurants. "We're certainly encouraging our restaurants to bring that conversation to the forefront," Joel Yashinsky, Burger King's chief marketing officer, told Fox News Digital. "We really want to make that real." AMERICA'S FAVORITE FAST-FOOD CHAIN NAMED: MCDONALD'S WINS HEARTS BUT NOT BEST BURGER, SURVEY SAYS That means working with franchise operators "to really think about how we can communicate very clearly to the guests that they do rule," Yashinsky said. But those interactions can't feel forced, he added. "It has to be authentic," he said. "We can't force it, but we are trying to, obviously, encourage that type of engagement to take place because we are truly trying to live it and mean it." KFC UNVEILS RADICALLY DIFFERENT RESTAURANT IN MAJOR COMEBACK PUSH The "You Rule" slogan was introduced in 2022. The newest catchphrase, "There's a New King and It's You," was introduced earlier this year. Burger King leadership has been talking with general managers about how to make that philosophy a "natural engagement" with guests, Yashinsky said. "The guest does rule," he said, "and we need to make sure that we acknowledge that." Burger King isn't the only fast-food chain to make a signature interaction with customers part of its approach to hospitality. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Chick-fil-A has become known for employees responding to customers with "my pleasure," a phrase closely associated with the chain's approach to customer service. At Burger King, part of instilling its own hospitality philosophy begins with employee training. Burger King employees are required to attend "Burger King University," which once had a physical campus at the chain's Miami headquarters, according to the Miami Herald. Today, however, the instructional program is solely online. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS An emphasis is placed on being hospitable, Yashinsky said. "If we can give an authentic greeting and a welcome and a smile, it goes a long way," he said. Making guests feel like they rule, however, doesn't mean employees can fulfill every request, including restrictions on when certain menu items can be sold. articles.title: Gyanesh Kumar: Police detain opposition leaders in Delhi demanding election commission chief's resignation
articles.summary: Opposition leaders have alleged that CEC Gyanesh Kumar manipulated voter rolls to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party during elections.
articles.body:
Police in Delhi detained several opposition lawmakers as they tried to march demanding the chief election commissioner resign over a controversial voter roll revision.

Main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka and other MPs were forced into a police bus. Released shortly after, they resumed their march and began a sit-in near Election Commission headquarters.

It is the latest escalation in a growing row over a nationwide revision of voter rolls.

Opposition parties accuse Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of overseeing a process that could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), an allegation both the BJP and Election Commission have rejected.

"Some of the MPs tried to take some other roads to the Election Commission building. We have officers stationed at multiple points, from where the protesters were picked up in buses and taken to different police stations," Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police Manjeet Sheoran told the BBC. The police did not disclose how many lawmakers had been detained. The opposition said 237 MPs from a range of parties participated in the march.

Tuesday's protest came just four days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a Gen Z-backed online satirical movement, organised demonstrations in Mumbai and Delhi, also demanding the CEC's resignation. The group has described those demonstrations as the beginning of a nationwide campaign and has called for another round of protests on 10 October.

At the centre of the controversy is the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

The exercise began in the eastern state of Bihar in June 2025 before being expanded to other parts of the country. The Election Commission says the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters from electoral rolls. More than 130 million names have so far been removed from draft voter lists nationwide.

Opposition parties and activists allege that many eligible voters have been wrongly excluded and accuse the poll body of conducting the process improperly.

The campaign against Kumar gathered momentum after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper reported that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over a 10-month period to decisions and orders they said had been issued in the Election Commission's name without their knowledge.

According to the report, the objections related to issues including additions and deletions from voter rolls, access to the voter database and the security of electoral data. Some concerns were linked directly to the electoral roll revision programme.

The Election Commission, a three-member body comprising the chief election commissioner and two election commissioners, defended its decision-making process, saying differing views were part of institutional functioning and that decisions had ultimately been taken unanimously.

The revelations nevertheless triggered a political backlash, with opposition leaders intensifying calls for Kumar's resignation.

Security was tightened around the Election Commission headquarters on Tuesday, with police barricading roads along the route between parliament and the commission's office.

Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge described three demands as "non-negotiable": Kumar's resignation, cancellation of the SIR exercise and a return to paper ballot voting.

Mocking the election chief, Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in India's lower house of parliament, tweeted: "Gyanesh, it's done, bro. Time to resign."

BJP MP Sambit Patra described them as a "sponsored attempt" to bring about a change of power through "anarchy". He accused opposition parties of seeking to undermine constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission.

The controversy has also reached India's Supreme Court, which has asked both the federal government and the Election Commission to respond to a petition alleging that Kumar took key decisions without the approval of the two other election commissioners.

The petition argues that Kumar exercised powers that belong to the commission collectively and seeks a ruling that any such actions were unauthorised.

The court indicated that Election Commission decisions must be taken either unanimously or by majority vote and suggested that decisions could be set aside if found to have bypassed that process. However, it declined to suspend Kumar at this stage, saying it would first hear the Election Commission's response and examine relevant records.

The BBC has contacted the Election Commission for comment on Tuesday's protest.

articles.title: Ship sinks and crew missing after Black Sea drone attack
articles.summary: It is not clear who is behind the attacks which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea as part of its war against Ukraine.
articles.body:
A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say.

A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its 18 crew were rescued.

Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine.

Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks were "unacceptable".

Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said.

The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. Named the Alfa Watan, it was a Turkish-owned general cargo ship and was reportedly heading for Sulina, Romania.

It is not clear what the Alfa Watan was carrying or how many people were on board.

A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. A search operation has been launched.

Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain.

Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan.

Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law".

He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable."

He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning.

"Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning."

"Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable."

Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea.

A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media.

On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title: Your feed isn't random. The algorithm is built to keep you angry, anxious and scrolling
articles.summary: In most Indian homes there used to be one person who read the newspaper properly, front to back, in order, and woe betide anyone who pulled out the sports
articles.body: In most Indian homes there used to be one person who read the newspaper properly, front to back, in order, and woe betide anyone who pulled out the sports page before he was done. The front page came first, with its riots and rail accidents and ministers saying things they would deny in the evening.Then came the edit page, where someone calmer explained what all that noise actually meant. Then the letters section, where a retired schoolteacher from Medinipur would disagree, very politely, with a retired bank manager from Pune.At the very end there was the crossword, filled in slowly with a blunt pencil while the tea went cold. When the last clue was cracked, the paper was folded, tucked under a cushion, and the reader got up to shave. The world had been terrible that morning, as it usually is, but the paper knew when to stop, and so did he.We wake up to a war zone every dayNow look at how most of us begin the day. We wake up, reach for the phone before our eyes are fully open, and start scrolling. Within a few minutes we have seen a video from a war zone, a scandal from some state capital, a clash inside a lift in Noida filmed on someone’s phone, and a post written with the sole aim of making us disgusted. Before our feet have touched the floor, the heart is beating faster, the mind is running ahead, and a vague sense of dread has settled in for the day.Nothing has happened to us, yet we feel as if a lot has. This is not because the world suddenly became worse. It is the result of a change in design, a change in how news reaches us, and to understand why the phone leaves us so tired and so angry, we have to understand what the old newspaper did and what the feed took away.The newspaper was a bundle. The front page gave you the problem, the edit page gave you an argument about it, the letters page gave you a fight over it, and the crossword gave you permission to put it all down. Each part had a job, and together they walked you through the bad news and then out of it.You were upset, then you understood a little, then you heard other people argue, and then you were done. Psychologists would call that closure. Your father simply called it finishing the paper.The feed kept only the front page. It threw away the edit page, the letters and the crossword, and then it did something cleverer and crueller: it put the front page on loop. There is no last page anymore. A newspaper came every morning and ended on Page 16.The feed comes in an endless scroll that never ends, and that ending was removed on purpose. Aza Raskin, the designer who invented infinite scrolling in 2006, has since said publicly that he regrets it. His point was simple. When you remove the natural places where a person would pause, you also remove the moments when they might decide to stop. Your thumb keeps going because nothing ever tells it to rest.Your feed wants you enraged, not informedThe next thing to understand is what the feed wants from you. It does not want you informed; and it certainly does not want you calm. It wants your attention, for as long as possible, because your attention is what it sells.The quickest way to grab attention is to excite or upset you, so the feed is built for arousal, not resolution. A calm, satisfied person closes the app and goes to make breakfast. An agitated person keeps scrolling. The machine learns this very quickly and serves more of whatever agitates.So you get every city’s crime, every flood, every atrocity, every outrage, everything that has gone wrong anywhere, all of it, all day, and none of it comes with a way to do anything about it. You get the pain of the entire world with no path out of it.Your body takes all this personally. Deep inside the brain is a small almond-shaped part called the amygdala, which works like a smoke alarm. When it senses danger, it rings loudly, and it does not check whether the danger is in your room or on a screen 2,000 kilometres away.It sends the alarm to the body, which releases stress hormones, cortisol and adrenaline, the same chemicals our ancestors needed when a tiger stepped out of the forest. Those chemicals prepare you to fight or to run. But you are sitting on your bed, holding a phone. There is no tiger and nowhere to run, so the chemicals have nowhere to go. They stay in your system, and you go on scrolling, and the alarm rings again and again.Complete mental breakdown is where we are at…Done once, this is harmless. Done every day for years, it wears you down. Sleep gets worse. Small things start to irritate you. You feel tired without having done anything tiring.The part of the brain right behind your forehead, the prefrontal cortex, which acts like the sensible elder in the family who tells you to think before you speak, gets pushed aside whenever you are in that heated state.Over time it becomes harder to concentrate, harder to control impulses, and easier to snap. People who live like this start reading ordinary things as threats, a neighbour's look, a colleague's message, a stranger's tone.This is not only a matter of morals or manners. It is a matter of health, and a lot of us are quietly unwell. There is a deeper injury too, and psychologists call it “learned helplessness”. It describes what happens when a person, or even an animal, faces something painful again and again and finds that nothing they do can stop it or escape it.After enough of this, the brain draws a conclusion. It decides that action is pointless, and it stops trying, even when a way out later appears. Human beings can handle a great deal of bad news as long as they can do something about it. Tell a village that the river is rising and they will build a wall. Tell them every day that rivers are rising in 40 countries, and that they can do nothing about any of them, and eventually they stop listening, or worse, they stop caring.That is our condition now. We are fully informed and completely stuck. We have become spectators at a fire that never goes out.Spectators get restless, and restless people get angry, and this is where we need to be careful with words.Outrage isn’t anger. One ends, the other doesn’tAnger and outrage are not the same thing. Anger, at its best, is useful. It tells you that a line has been crossed, and it gives you the energy to go and fix a specific problem. The parent who is angry about a broken streetlight writes to the municipality and gets it fixed. Outrage is anger with a loudspeaker, directed towards no one in particular. It is loud, and it asks you to do nothing except react.The platforms love outrage, and they have good reason to. A team of researchers led by William Brady, publishing in the journal PNAS, found that adding just one moral and emotional word to a post, words such as shame, hate or corrupt, made it roughly 20% more likely to be shared.The researchers explained why with a simple idea. Human beings are wired to show which side they are on, to signal to their group that they are good and the other lot are bad. Emotional, moral words catch our eye faster than plain facts do. And the platform's system notices which posts grab eyes fastest and pushes them to even more people.Outrage makes us want to believe in liesSo the most heated language gets the biggest reward, and everyone learns to speak a little more heatedly tomorrow. It is a loop.It gets worse. Further research by psychologists Brady, Molly Crockett and colleagues found that sources of misinformation tend to stir up more outrage than trustworthy news outlets do.Outrage also makes people less likely to check whether something is true. So the angriest stories are often the least reliable ones, and they are precisely the stories people share without even opening them. The lie travels in a jet plane while the truth is still looking for e-rickshaw.Then there is the strangest trick of all, which is that sharing feels like doing. When you repost an angry video or add a furious comment to someone's post, you get a small feeling of having acted, of having stood up for something. It costs you nothing and changes nothing, but for a moment it feels like a duty performed. Call it fake catharsis.A quote-tweet is action without the action. Ten years ago we laughed at this and called it slacktivism. Today, for millions of people, it is the only activism they do.And here is the part we rarely talk about. Rage with nowhere to go does not evaporate. Psychologists who study what they call displaced aggression have shown that when tension builds up and finds no outlet, it gets stored and later spent on whoever happens to be nearest and weakest.The delivery boy who is ten minutes late. The stranger in the comments. The cousin in the family WhatsApp group who forwarded the wrong thing. The minority of the week, whoever the feed has decided that is. The algorithm manufactures the rage, and our near and dear ones pay the price.There are people who are very happy with this arrangement. A population that feels angry and helpless is a population looking for an explanation, and grievance always goes looking for an ideology.Societal frustration turned into big businessPolitical and commercial players who have one to sell find willing buyers. They take that vague, floating anger and give it a shape, a target and a slogan, and in doing so they turn a society's frustration into a business that grows with every scroll. A country can survive a lot of bad news. It struggles to survive a population that has been trained to hate on schedule.If all this is hard on adults, it is much harder on children. A teenager's brain is still under construction. They are working out who they are, how to read faces, how to make up after a fight, how to sit with a difficult feeling until it passes.Social psychologist Jonathan Haidt, in his book, The Anxious Generation, argues that between 2010 and 2012 childhood itself changed shape. It moved from a play-based childhood, spent outdoors with friends, to a phone-based childhood, spent alone with a screen. He points to four kinds of damage.Time spent with friends in person dropped by roughly half from 2012 onwards, so children got less practice at the messy, real business of getting along. Sleep suffered, because notifications and late-night scrolling cut into the hours a growing brain needs most. Attention broke into little pieces, so sitting with one hard problem for a long time became harder. And the endless comparison, with perfect faces and public counts of likes and views, made a whole generation feel permanently not good enough.The numbers from the United States, where this has been studied most closely, are frightening. Suicide rates among children aged 10 to 14 more than doubled between 2010 and 2020, and hospital admissions for self-harm rose sharply from the early 2010s.Researchers still argue over how much of this the phone alone explains, but the timing has made a lot of parents and governments sit up. We are showing children a world on fire before they have even learnt to cross the road alone. Anxiety mixed with powerlessness, at the very age when a person is deciding who they are, is a cocktail nobody should be pouring for a child.Why governments are intervening globallyThis is why the world is changing its mind about tech companies. For about two decades, roughly from 2000 to 2019, governments let platforms police themselves, with community guidelines and an age box that any ten-year-old could tick.From around 2020, Europe began asking for transparency, and its Digital Services Act now requires the biggest platforms to offer users a feed that is not built on profiling them, with fines of up to 6% of a company's global turnover for failing.Now a third phase has begun, in which governments are no longer only asking platforms to explain their design. They are starting to change it.Australia has gone furthest. Its Social Media Minimum Age law came into force on 10 December 2025 and requires platforms to take reasonable steps to keep children under 16 off their services.It is aimed squarely at platforms that use the features we have been talking about, recommendation systems, infinite scrolling, likes and disappearing stories. In the first few weeks, platforms removed about 47 lakh underage Australian accounts. Companies that fail to comply can be fined up to A$109.2 million, roughly ₹600 crore.In September this year Australia went a step further with a Digital Duty of Care bill. The idea is borrowed from workplace safety law: just as a factory owner must keep the shop floor safe for workers, a platform must keep its space safe for users.The bill targets the risky design features directly, the recommending algorithms, the endless feeds, the counts of likes, and the content that disappears. Under what the government calls: “My Feed, My Way”, platforms must let people switch off algorithmic recommendations entirely and choose a simple feed, in time order, showing only the accounts they have chosen to follow.Prime Minister Anthony Albanese summed it up neatly: “It’s not about giving government control. It’s about giving people control.” That is the key. Australia is not asking for less content. It is asking for a feed with an ending.Others are following. Britain is considering a ban on social media for those under 16, and for 16 and 17 year olds, a default curfew that would switch off feeds between midnight and 6 in the morning. And in India, parliamentary panels have begun discussing platform accountability, algorithmic transparency and user safety, though no firm law has yet taken shape.The 'diversity' powder kegWe cannot afford to take our time. India has hundreds of millions of people who came online through cheap mobile data, many of them for the first time, and many of them in a phone-first world without ever having had a newspaper habit to compare it with.We are also among the most diverse countries on earth, and diversity is exactly the kind of soil in which outrage grows fastest. We have already seen forwarded rumours turn into mobs, and online fury turn into real fights on real streets.An engine built to reward rage, running unchecked in a crowded and plural country, is not just a mental health problem. It is a question of whether neighbours can keep living next to each other.The good news is that the fix does not need censorship. Nobody needs to decide which opinions are allowed. What India needs is what Australia is attempting: make platforms explain how their algorithms choose what we see, give every user the right to switch to a plain feed of the people they actually follow, and bring back the stopping points that were removed on purpose. These are design rules, not speech rules.It is tempting to say all of this comes down to willpower, that people should simply use their phones less. But we did not tell factory workers to breathe less when the air was toxic. We made laws about the chimneys. We did not ask labourers to be braver about falling from scaffolding. We made safety rules for construction sites.A feed designed by some of the cleverest engineers in the world to keep you from stopping is not a fair fight for a tired adult, let alone a 13-year-old. The problem is in the design, so the solution has to be in the design too.The old newspaper was not perfect. It was often biased, sometimes boring, and occasionally wrong. But it did one thing that we have forgotten to value. It showed you the troubles of the world, helped you think about them, let you argue about them, and then gave you a crossword and sent you on your way.Somewhere tonight, someone will fold a paper and put it under a cushion. The news inside it is just as bad as the news on your phone. The difference is that it ends.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi deterrence against Houthis: What that means
articles.summary: Islamabad says its role is defensive, but Riyadh’s offensive in Yemen tests how long it can stay out of the fight.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan — For the first time since it was signed in August, the Mecca pact between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye is now in force.

At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday, the pact’s top committee agreed to deploy Pakistani and Turkish forces to the kingdom, which is backing an offensive against Yemen’s Houthis.

“The Committee decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the Parties,” said a joint statement shared by Pakistan’s Foreign Office.

The statement did not specify the size or role of the forces.

Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Major General Turki al-Malki said 100 fighter jets were supporting a Yemeni government counteroffensive to retake territory seized by the Houthis last month.

Hours after the meeting, Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistani forces were already playing a part.

“The forces of Turkiye and Pakistan are playing a supporting role. We are definitely involved in reconnaissance and such things, but the combat is practically being conducted by Saudi Arabia’s own forces, and they are the ones retaking those areas,” Asif told Geo News, speaking from Riyadh on Monday night.

That leaves Pakistan in a defensive role alongside a Saudi offensive. Analysts told Al Jazeera that it raises a question Islamabad has yet to answer publicly: How long can it stay out of the actual fighting?

Pakistan already had a military presence in Saudi Arabia. It has trained Saudi military personnel since 1967, with a 1982 agreement formalising the deputation of troops to the kingdom.

A declassified CIA assessment from June 1985 estimated that 13,000 to 14,000 Pakistanis were serving in the Saudi army, including an armoured brigade at Tabuk. During the 1990-91 Gulf War, Pakistan also sent a large contingent to the kingdom for defensive duties.

Pakistan also signed the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia in September 2025 , which treats aggression against either country as aggression against both.

In April, Riyadh confirmed that a Pakistani force , including fighter and support aircraft, had arrived at King Abdulaziz Air Base in the Eastern Province.

Pakistan has never disclosed how many of its troops are in Saudi Arabia.

In September, Lieutenant-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, director general of the military’s media wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), told the Saudi outlet Arab News that Pakistani forces were already deployed to protect the kingdom and its holy sites.

“I would like to underscore here the word ‘physically’,” Chaudhry said. “We will go to any extent.”

ISPR did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on the deployment agreed upon in Riyadh.

On Tuesday, Pakistan’s Ministry of Information said in a post on X that the country’s commitment to the security of the holy sites and the kingdom was not negotiable.

“The operational details of the actualisation of the collective deterrence are a matter of operational confidentiality and may not be made subject of media speculation,” the ministry said.

Asif said Turkish forces were also present, but Ankara has not publicly confirmed any deployment.

“There is no publicly acknowledged standing Turkish deployment in Saudi Arabia,” Gokhan Ereli, an international relations expert at Istanbul’s Ibn Haldun University, told Al Jazeera.

Ereli noted that under Article 92 of Turkiye’s constitution, the authority to send troops abroad rests with the parliament, which has yet to ratify the Mecca pact.

Dania Thafer, executive director of the Gulf International Forum, said Riyadh wants the pact to carry real weight .

“Saudi Arabia is trying to turn the Mecca Pact from a political declaration into a deterrent,” she told Al Jazeera.

For now, she said, Riyadh mainly wants Pakistan and Turkiye to help defend Saudi territory and reinforce its air and missile defences, showing that another attack is no longer only a Saudi-Houthi matter. The Houthis have attacked multiple Saudi cities and facilities, including the East West Pipeline that Riyadh has been using to export oil amid Iranian restrictions on transit through the Strait of Hormuz during the ongoing war waged by the US.

Saudi authorities said two of its airports had been hit on Monday evening, injuring at least three people.

But Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman’s account of the meeting went further than what Thafer suggested.

“The committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures within the framework of the Alliance in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them,” he wrote on X.

“‘All those responsible’ is intentionally ambiguous. It tells the Houthis that Saudi Arabia may go beyond intercepting missiles and strike any actor or infrastructure enabling those attacks. It is also simultaneously warning external sponsors that Riyadh is watching the entire support network,” she said.

However, Pakistani officials have been more cautious.

“The document itself says, first, that it is defensive in nature. It has no offensive agenda,” Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said at a news conference in Islamabad on October 2.

Tughral Yamin, a retired brigadier and senior associate at Islamabad’s Institute of Policy Studies, said Pakistan’s contribution was likely to be specialised rather than large.

“Pakistan is most likely going to beef up its existing presence with air defence units, drones, battlefield communication systems and offensive cyber specialists, men from the corps of engineers to lay and lift mines, some special service troops. Nothing more than that, I would say,” he told Al Jazeera.

Ereli expects Turkiye’s role to be similarly limited.

“The realistic response would be calibrated and mostly non-ground. That means diplomatic coordination, intelligence sharing, emergency resupply of air defence, drones and electronic warfare, and perhaps naval or air-defence assets,” he said.

Thafer said two campaigns were now running side by side.

“There are really two concentric operations taking place: one is defending Saudi Arabia; the second is changing the military balance inside Yemen so the Houthis cannot continue attacking Saudi territory from a position of growing strength,” she said.

Pakistan has not said publicly where its role stops.

Asked by reporters in Rome on September 30 whether Pakistani forces had joined strikes in Yemen, Asif did not answer directly.

“I’m not going into detail, but obviously, when I say that we are bound by this arrangement to defend Saudi Arabia, that means whatever means are available at our disposal, they’ll be available to Saudi Arabia also,” he said.

Pakistan has faced this question before.

In April 2015, its parliament unanimously resolved that “Pakistan should maintain neutrality in the Yemen conflict so as to be able to play a proactive diplomatic role to end the crisis”. But the resolution also pledged that Pakistan would stand with Saudi Arabia if its territorial integrity were violated or the holy sites threatened.

Monday’s joint statement justified the deployment in similar terms and condemned the attempted targeting of Mecca and Medina .

Tehran, though, is watching closely . On Sunday, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran hoped reports of a Pakistani deployment for war in Yemen were untrue. He warned that any new intervention would only complicate the situation.

At the same news conference last week, Dar said he had raised the pact with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in New York in September, on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly.

“I made them aware that we are in a defence pact, and as Muslims, we have to honour it, and God willing, we will,” he said.

He said the Iranian leaders had suggested engaging the Houthis politically rather than through military action. Monday’s statement made no mention of a political track.

Javad Heiran-Nia, an analyst with the Persian Gulf Studies Group in Tehran, said Iran draws a clear distinction between defending Saudi territory and infrastructure and attacking the Houthis in Yemen.

“In general, if Pakistan’s deployment is purely defensive and limited to the protection of Saudi installations, Tehran can tolerate it. However, if Pakistan joins offensive operations against the Houthis, Iran regards it as a red line, since it views the Houthis as part of its strategic depth in the Arabian Peninsula,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Currently, Pakistan’s mediation has shifted from neutrality to management of conflicting interests, and its credibility is highly fragile,” he added.

Yamin, too, said the onus was on Islamabad.

“Pakistan needs to draw its redlines carefully to prevent its troops getting involved in combat operations against the Houthis. So the question should [be] not how will they get involved but how can they prevent getting involved,” he said.

Much depends on what Riyadh wants from Yemen.

“Riyadh probably wants a short, high-intensity campaign that restores deterrence rather than another open-ended Yemen war,” Thafer said.

But Yemeni government forces this week said they were no longer limiting their ambitions to regaining territory lost to the Houthis in recent weeks, and were in fact aiming to retake capital Sanaa, held by the Iran-backed group since 2014.

“Military campaigns are determined by objectives: securing Saudi territory and Bab al-Mandab could potentially be limited,” Thafer said. “Trying to fundamentally defeat the Houthis or retake Sanaa would be a very different and potentially much longer war.”

articles.title: K-8 attack jets, military vehicles spotted at new China-Laos air base: Report
articles.summary: China is expanding its military presence in Southeast Asia, with satellite imagery showing light attack aircraft and military vehicles at a newly
articles.body: China is expanding its military presence in Southeast Asia, with satellite imagery showing light attack aircraft and military vehicles at a newly established China-Laos joint training facility near Vientiane, according to reports.The images, taken on September 30 by commercial satellite provider Vantor, show what security analysts believe are eight K-8 light attack jets and more than two dozen support vehicles on a runway that is still under construction, Reuters reported.China opened its first overseas military base in Djibouti in 2017 and has also developed a military presence at Cambodia’s Ream naval facility. The new Ban Keun airport is located in northwestern Vientiane province, about 45 km north of the Laotian capital, Vientiane. Situated at the centre of the Indochina peninsula, the airfield previously served as a tactical support site within the US network of airstrips in Laos during the Laotian Civil War and the Vietnam War era, before ceasing active operations after the conflicts.The facility at Ban Keun, about 50 km north of the Laotian capital, was announced by China and Laos on September 29. China’s defence ministry said the centre would support training for Laotian air force pilots and would be operated by both sides.Reuters reported that the images also show extensive construction around the runway, with analysts watching for signs of air-defence systems, ammunition and fuel storage and surveillance facilities.Rachel Vandenbrink, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told Reuters the location was “likely more about a target of opportunity than filling an obvious operational need”.“Laos does have some geostrategic value as an accessible foothold in mainland Southeast Asia, given its shared border with China and infrastructure links, including (its) railway,” she said.The K-8 aircraft, also known as the Hongdu JL-8, are used for training and light attack missions and are operated by both China and Laos, according to Reuters. Laos has four of the aircraft, based on the International Institute for Strategic Studies’ annual assessment.China’s defence ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment, while the Lao embassy in Bangkok and Laos’ foreign ministry also did not immediately respond.AFP reported that Joshua Kurlantzick of the council on foreign relations described the facility as China’s “first air force base that China has abroad”, while cautioning that further overseas facilities could follow.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cornell faculty senate introduces no-confidence resolution over handling of alleged 2024 sexual assault
articles.summary: ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University faculty introduced a resolution declaring a no-confidence vote in the university administration’s handling of the alleged 2024 sexual assault at a fraternity house.
articles.body: ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University faculty introduced a resolution declaring a no-confidence vote in the university administration’s handling of the alleged 2024 sexual assault at a fraternity house. The resolution was submitted to the University Faculty Committee on Monday evening, according to a copy obtained by NBC News. “That the Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University,” the resolution, which is less than half a page, says. The measure is expected to be considered by the faculty senate, which meets Oct. 14, according to a statement from faculty senator Paul Ortiz. “The goal is to really force systemic change,” Ortiz, a professor of labor history, said in a statement. Ortiz added that “students have been telling us stories they don’t feel safe, and this has been going on for a number of years” and called the situation a “systemic problem.” He reiterated that the senate was not “targeting any individual” but that the students and faculty “have been unsatisfied with the response.” “Women need to feel safe,” he said. In a statement accompanying the resolution, the faculty sponsors said “numerous Cornell colleagues” had approached them demanding action, while students had told faculty they were “upset, fearful for their personal safety,” and wanted the Ivy League school to address sexual assault on campus. Cornell alumni had also contacted faculty members and shared “their own traumatic stories as students,” the statement added. Cornell declined to comment. The proposed no-confidence resolution marks an escalation in pressure on Cornell and its administration following national scrutiny over how the case was handled. Last month, a former student identified as Jane Doe sued the university and seven current and former students in connection with the alleged sexual assault. She alleges that in October 2024 she was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members while she was impaired by alcohol, ketamine and marijuana. The woman’s allegations have made national headlines for days and prompted protests on the university’s campus after widespread criticism that the university and local officials did not do enough to investigate the woman’s allegations. Anne Marie Elizabeth Brady, a Faculty Senate member and research director for the university’s Industrial and Labor Relations Workers Institute, said the resolution came together “quickly” in recent days. “If I was a woman on Cornell’s campus, I’d run in the other direction,” she said. “Because I’m not sure Cornell is there to protect the students the way they should be.” Brady said that Cornell’s decision to discipline the seven men accused of wrongdoing instead of passing on the case to outside law enforcement “feels like a cover-up to me.” “If I’m a betting woman, I suspect they didn’t do that because they wanted to keep it secret,” she said. “They wanted to manage the story.” If the Faculty Senate passes the resolution, Brady said, it will then prompt a series of discussions between faculty and Cornell’s leadership for policies affecting sexual assault. Similar action was taken last year following years of campus protests of the war in Gaza. Brady says those recommendations have largely been ignored. “If the administration came out and said: ‘you know what? we screwed up, we did A, B, and C wrong. We failed this student, we failed all our students through this process and these are the concrete ways and steps we are going to take to change,’” she said. “If they did that? That goes so far.” Adam Reiss and Maggie Vespa reported from Ithaca; Matt Lavietes reported from New York City.

articles.title: After a re-energizing year, Chanel takes flight
articles.summary: A year after his highly-rated debut as the new artistic director of Chanel, Matthieu Blazy showed that despite the rave reviews and frenzied shoppers, he hasn’t lost sight of how it all began.
articles.body: A year after his highly-rated debut as the new artistic director of Chanel, Matthieu Blazy showed that despite the rave reviews and frenzied shoppers, he hasn’t lost sight of how it all began. On Monday night, the designer presented an ode to the house’s founder, Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel through a collection that celebrated — and, importantly, offered clothing for — the many stages of a woman’s life. Opening the show, model Dyanira Hurbuscher walked in a sheer look — a bra hinting at the boning seen in Edwardian-era corsetry, but completely softened and unrestricted (Gabrielle famously rejected the stiff fashion rules of her time). Hurbuscher carried one of Madam Chanel’s personal 2.55 bags, plucked out of the Patrimoine archives. This piece of fashion history acted as a bookend, appearing again in the collection’s final look — honoring fashion’s matriarch from start to finish. But last night’s runway wasn’t meant to be a history lesson, Blazy said in show notes, this was about giving women the clothing they need at each chapter: “Throughout their lives, women become multiple selves, different faces of the same coin. It’s like a game of exquisite corpse, where one identity leads to another. It’s about the women within a woman. And here, it’s about one woman, Gabrielle, who then became Chanel.” Quiet luxury be damned It’s true, a woman may inhabit the same body all her life, but she is far from static, rather always shifting and transforming — adopting new roles or playing different characters within the same skin and bones. In Blazy’s telling, underwear, whimsical tulle skirts, color-clashing patterns and playful (and detachable) clown collars — light, youthful and buoyant in spirit — serve as the beginning of the story, making way for clothes that a woman with a job and responsibilities might need to get through the day while looking great and not at all quiet: pinstripe trousers, soft tailoring, enriched with textural details like the often-present feathery floral brooches, and a couple of takes on a men’s gilet cinched in at the waist. Later, clothing for life’s joyful milestones: silk 1930s-style dresses, sequins and an opulent black billowing gown. Of course, signature skirt suits and tweed appeared throughout but there was technical innovation here in the form of what the designer is calling “smocked tweed,” a stretchy more malleable iteration of a Chanel classic which he playfully likened to sportswear. Many of these archetypal suits were also worn with nothing underneath — no longer uptight bourgeois armor, but rather designs meant to be worn “lightly as perfume.” Birds — namely swifts, swallows, cranes and geese — served as a motif, popping up within the invitations, decorating some of the garments, and soaring above our heads during the show. The idea for the set came to Blazy while on holiday in the south of Italy, where he was inspired by an area of Calabria that acts a natural reserve for birds. Bringing it back his founder he said, “Ultimately, Chanel took off, and each step she took led to her being free, like a bird.” The energy both outside and within the Grand Palais reflected this spirit, with guests including Dua Lipa, Nicole Kidman and Pedro Pascal spotted dancing in their seats to Britney Spears’ “Gimme More.” Blazy, 42, who cannot resist injecting a mood-boosting millennial banger into his show music, was clearly having fun this season. And why wouldn’t he after such a successful first year? As the finale of models filed backstage, the designer came out to take his bow, light on his feet as he waved to the audience before running back to his team, arms wide open ready for whatever comes next. articles.title: Husband who drugged and raped wife for 20 years makes witness statement
articles.summary: Jurors were told that the man had given a "detailed" statement about "what he says happened".
articles.body:
A man who has admitted drugging and raping his wife without her knowledge for more than 20 years has provided a witness statement about "what he says happened", a jury was told.

The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's right to anonymity, had also been accused of inviting 13 other men to abuse her from 2018 until November 2025.

The man, in his 60s and from the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, had initially denied the charges but pleaded guilty last month to 60 offences, including rape and administering a substance with intent.

A jury was sworn in at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court in early September but the case has since been delayed for legal and practical reasons.

One of the co-defendants - 59-year-old Keith Fotheringham from Dundee, Scotland – has also pleaded guilty to several offences.

Earlier the nine women and three men of the jury, plus two female reserve jurors, were invited into court and provided with an update by Judge Maurice Greene.

They had already been told at a previous hearing that the husband had admitted 60 offences and would no longer be part of the trial as a defendant.

However, Judge Greene said: "What's been happening is that the husband has now made a statement about what he says happened.

"That statement is a long statement and that has been disclosed to all defence counsel and it contains a lot of detail."

The judge told jurors the statement contained "lots of pages and lots of documents" and that lawyers in the case were "going through it carefully", which was ongoing work.

The jury were asked to return on Monday 19 October when the prosecution case against the remaining 12 defendants is due to open.

articles.title: UK police arrest British national linked to airbase incident
articles.summary: 22-year old British national arrested on suspicion of a terror offence after other suspects released on bail.
articles.body:
British police have arrested a 22-year old British national on suspicion of a terror offence linked to the security incident near a UK airbase hosting US warplanes on September 27.

Counter Terrorism Police say the individual is connected with “activity that took place close to RAF Fairford.”

In a statement, police said the arrest had been made “on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts”.

“This remains ⁠a live investigation and our specialist teams continue to pursue ⁠multiple lines of enquiry into ⁠the circumstances surrounding events near RAF Fairford,” Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing said.

The latest arrest is the seventh connected to the incident, which remains largely unexplained, over the past two weeks.

Five British men in their twenties were detained near the perimeter of the base in the early hours of September 27.

Police said they had found a supply of gasoline in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.

On Thursday, a 25-year-old British-Iranian man was arrested in London.

All six have been released on bail under investigation.

The US moved its B-52 and B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford on Sunday, though it’s unclear whether the move is connected to the arrests.

RAF Fairford has served as a stopping point for US bombers participating in the war against Iran, which began more than seven months ago, on February 28.

Located roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, the base has since been rumoured to be the target of a “terror” plot involving Tehran.

On Monday, US President Trump said his administration withdrew B-1 bombers from the site because of what he described as “some threats”.

“We had a threat, and if we’re going to be threatened, we would just move them, and that sort of alleviates that,” he told reporters, adding the people who made the threat “would be linked to Iran,” without elaborating.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK sees, “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident, without providing details.

Iran has denied involvement, but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

articles.title: Florida couple’s colorful Sarasota cottage village houses 17 small businesses; a 324-apartment plan threatened demolition, but owners canceled the sale and took the property off market
articles.summary: A cluster of colorful cottages along Fruitville Road in downtown Sarasota has been spared from demolition, at least for now.
articles.body: A cluster of colorful cottages along Fruitville Road in downtown Sarasota has been spared from demolition, at least for now. The Historic Downtown Village, home to 17 locally owned businesses, was under contract to be sold to a developer who planned to replace the bungalows with a 324-unit apartment complex. In early October, owners Alex and Marlene Lancaster told tenants the deal had fallen through and that they would continue owning and managing the property, taking it off the market entirely. The reversal ends months of uncertainty for shop and restaurant owners who had been weighing relocation options, according to reports by Sarasota Magazine and MySuncoast.A village of small businesses in bright cottagesThe Historic Downtown Village sits on about 3.44 acres between Fruitville Road, Fourth Street, North Osprey Avenue and Gillespie Avenue. The site is filled with small, brightly painted cottages that house a mix of restaurants, cafes, boutiques and services. Among the tenants are FAM Cuisine, The Breakfast House, Siegfried’s Restaurant and Biergarten, The Artful Giraffe and Discover Sarasota Tours, all of which have become part of the daily rhythm for downtown residents and visitors.For many of these business owners, the cottages are more than just a lease. They describe the village as a community where customers know their names and where generations of families have worked. One owner told MySuncoast that the restaurant has been a constant in their life since childhood, with family members returning after college to keep the business running. That sense of continuity is what makes the threat of displacement so emotionally charged.The cottages themselves have become a local landmark. Their modest scale and vibrant colours stand in contrast to the larger buildings and parking lots that dominate many nearby corridors. For residents, the village offers a walkable collection of places to eat, shop and gather, all within a few steps of one another.A 324-unit proposal and the prospect of demolitionThe potential sale emerged earlier in 2026, when Tennessee-based Bristol Development Group approached the Lancasters with a proposal to redevelop the site. The plan, known as 1899 Fruitville, called for a five-story apartment building with six levels of structured parking and 324 residential units. The existing cottages would have been demolished to make way for the new complex, which also included amenities such as a gym, clubhouse and pool.The project went through the city’s review process, with the Planning Board unanimously approving two zoning adjustments tied to the design in August. As part of that approval, Bristol committed to preserving two grand oak trees and creating a publicly accessible green space at the northeast corner of the property. The proposal also included wider sidewalks, shade trees, underground utilities and drainage improvements intended to enhance the pedestrian environment along the block.For tenants, however, those public benefits did not offset the loss of their homes and businesses. Many said they were not surprised by the news, given the site’s location and zoning, but the idea of leaving a place with deep history brought up strong emotions. Some began actively looking for new locations, while others explored the possibility of moving the cottages themselves to a different site, as per reports.Tenants weigh relocation and resistanceAs the development review process unfolded, tenants found themselves in a difficult position. They needed to plan for the possibility of moving, but they did not know when they might have to leave or whether they could afford comparable space in downtown Sarasota. Laetitia Kepecz of FAM Cuisine said, as per Sarasota Magazine, that she had heard rumors that the deal might fall through but did not trust the news until confirmation arrived directly from the Lancasters.Kepecz further explained that finding another downtown location that would keep the restaurant close to its existing customers had seemed financially out of reach. Even when spaces were available, she said, the rents in downtown Sarasota made a move difficult to justify. The restaurant had been looking at options outside the downtown core, though she said they were open to anywhere that made sense. For now, she is relieved to have more time to figure out the future in a community they love.Some tenants took more concrete steps toward relocation. In July, Breakfast House owner Wendy Lee Goldberg purchased about an acre at 128 North Briggs Avenue, roughly a mile east near Fruitville Road and Tuttle Avenue. Her plan was to convert an existing house into the restaurant’s new home. She and neighbouring business owners were also exploring the idea of a Sarasota Bungalow Village, potentially moving several cottages onto the property and arranging businesses around a community green with shaded walkways, reported Sarasota Magazine.Owners cite confidentiality and end the saleIn an October 3 email to tenants, Alex and Marlene Lancaster said the purchase agreement was no longer in effect and that they intended to continue owning and managing the property. They wrote that they were not listing, marketing or seeking a buyer, and that the property was not being offered for sale. The email did not explain why the agreement ended, only that the contract was no longer active.The Lancasters also addressed their silence during the development review process. They said the buyer had approached them directly, rather than responding to a listing, and that a nondisclosure agreement prevented them from discussing the potential transaction with tenants or the public. They wrote that their lack of communication was not intended to create uncertainty or concern, but that they were contractually required to maintain confidentiality.Philip DiMaria of Kimley-Horn, who represented the project through the city’s review process, confirmed that the transaction did not go through, reported Sarasota Magazine. He said he hoped any future proposal would incorporate the public benefits that had been planned for this development, including the preserved trees and green space. For now, however, those features remain part of a proposal that will not move forward.What comes next for the cottage villageReal estate experts say the end of this deal may not end developer interest in the property. Mark Klecka, a realtor with Coldwell Banker Realty, noted that given the site’s location, zoning and previous redevelopment proposal, another developer is likely to approach the owners eventually. But for now, that remains a forecast rather than a certainty, as per Sarasota Magazine.The Lancasters told tenants their intention is to retain the property and provide the stability they had before the offer arrived. That message brought relief to business owners who had been living with the prospect of displacement for months. For now, the colorful cottages will continue to house the same mix of restaurants, shops and services that have defined the village for years.The story of the Historic Downtown Village reflects a broader tension in growing cities like Sarasota. On one side is the pressure to add housing density near employment centres and transit corridors. On the other is the desire to preserve small-scale, locally owned businesses and the character they bring to downtown neighbourhoods. The collapse of the 1899 Fruitville deal does not resolve that tension, but it does buy time for the cottage village and the people who depend on it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
