articles.title: 'Gen Z has risen up': Tens of thousands demand better education in France
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday, as unions and teachers joined high school students who for days have been de...
articles.body:
Tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday, as unions and teachers joined high school students who for days have been demanding better learning conditions in protests punctuated by violent confrontations.

Students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds since late September, complaining of missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures.

Unions, rights groups and the children have accused the authorities of using disproportionate force -- a police stun grenade tore the hand off one teenager on Monday and another youngster had his teeth knocked out last week after police fired a grenade launcher at his head.

At the Place de la Republique in central Paris, the savoury smell of grilled merguez sausages -- a French protest staple -- wafted over the crowd.

Two men in climbing gear scaled the nearby monument, where they unfurled a plastic banner reading "Neglected schools, sacrificed youth".

"Gen Z has risen up and wants to be heard," 19-year-old Lilia told AFP at a massive march in central Paris, adding she hoped the president would listen.

The unrest has erupted with just months to go before the 2027 election to choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with far-right veteran candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls despite a graft conviction.

"I'm afraid for my future," Selma, 15, told AFP without giving her surname, among the thousands marching in the country's second largest city of Marseille.

The interior ministry said 86,000 had already joined demonstrations across the rest of the country earlier Tuesday. The CGT union put the figure at 260,000 people.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu responded to the demonstrations, telling lawmakers in the National Assembly that there was "no room for tolerance of violence".

"Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings," he told parliament, adding it was a "lie" to suggest the government had ordered "police repression" against protesters.

While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have started fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police.

Police have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds.

The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement.

A 15-year-old lost a hand to a sting-ball grenade fired by riot officers in the northern town of Lens on Monday.

The prosecutor's office in the northeastern town of Metz meanwhile said he called for a police inquiry over a possible sexual assault on a minor younger than 15, after video footage circulated of what appeared to be a plainclothes policeman groping a female pupil he had detained.

The government has sought to address the grievances, while accusing the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of being behind the movement.

Veteran LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has strongly supported the protests, while calling for non-violent methods.

Thomas, a 17-year-old student from the Paris suburb of Val-de-Marne, said some of the classrooms at his school were short of desks and chairs while the bathrooms lacked doors, toilet paper and soap.

"We just want better conditions for studying," he told AFP.

Adults turned out in droves Tuesday to support the young demonstrators.

Standing outside a school in Rennes, in western France, teacher Romain Dubourg told AFP he and colleagues had "talked about the police brutality we've witnessed" and decided to show up for the pupils.

In the eastern city of Lyon, Sandrine Buteau was among dozens of parents who organised to support the youngsters.

"As adults, we're a bit like the security cordon," she said.

Lyon teacher Rindala Younes said she was present to help the students "convey their message peacefully".

"The high school students' demands are legitimate," she said.

Amnesty International late Monday said the French authorities should "put an end to the disproportionate police repression seen in recent days during student protests".

The police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said late Monday.

Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education ministry.

More than 5,000 people, 87 percent of them minors, have been arrested.

The prime minister's office said 85 teaching staff have also been injured.

articles.title: Canada has a plan to rebuild its army — Washington should hope it works
articles.summary: Ottawa has laid out a plan to convert the Canadian Army from a hollow force into one that is adapted to the contemporary battle space.
articles.body:
In September 1943, troops of the First Canadian Division carried out a daring attack on the Italian town of Potenza , enabling the British and American forces to turn what might have been a disastrous defeat into a significant victory. Fast forward 83 years, however, and it is reasonable to ask if today’s Canadian Army would once again be able to save the day in a major combat operation involving U.S. forces — or even to contribute meaningfully to such an operation in a distant battlespace.

At the moment, the answer is clearly no.

And the reason is obvious: At least since the end of the Cold War, the Canadian Army has been optimized for “contribution warfare” — that is, “for employment in multinational coalitions for operations other than large-scale, high-intensity combat.” That made sense during the post-Cold War unipolar moment when middle powers like Canada were primarily engaged in peacekeeping and counterinsurgency operations. But that moment has passed, and the army Canada currently possesses is no longer the Army Canada needs . Nor is it the army the U.S. needs Canada to have.

Recognizing this, Ottawa has laid out a plan to convert the Canadian Army from a hollow force into one that is adapted to the contemporary battle space. That plan, known as Inflection Point 2025 , calls for the creation of a warfighting army organized, trained and equipped for sustained major combat operations “against peer or near-peer adversaries.”

But, while Inflection Point is a good plan, so far that’s all it is: a plan. And, to paraphrase the immortal words of Robbie Burns, even the best laid plans of mice and men often go awry.

Canada’s ambitious plan may well go awry if Ottawa isn’t willing or able to do more than create a new organization chart. If it isn’t willing or able to invest in the recruitment, equipment, training and sustainment system necessary to stand up new Canadian combat units that are more than just repackaged hollow formations. There are good reasons to believe that such investments will not be forthcoming — at least not any time soon.

To start, there is the recruitment problem. Inflection Point assumes that the army’s strategic intake plan will not only make up the 3,000 soldier shortfall in last year’s overall recruiting numbers but also recruit the 8,500 more regular personnel it envisions by 2040. But that is a working assumption, not a given. And, if the past is prologue , there is little reason to believe that Canada can recruit, train and retain the personnel necessary to convert these assumptions into reality.

Then there’s the procurement problem. A Canadian Army unit deployed for either deterrence or warfighting purposes will need the very best equipment appropriate to the evolving battlespace. But Canada’s procurement system, even as recently reformed by the Carney government, is not built to deliver such equipment — and certainly not in a timely fashion. What it is built for is the satisfaction of politically motivated interests such as creating jobs in Canada and diversifying away from the U.S. arms industry that have little to do with providing the army with the equipment it needs to fight and win in the contemporary battlespace.

And even if Canada solves its procurement issue it will continue to face the related challenge of sustainment — building the stocks and supply lines capable of providing a division-sized unit with the ammunition, equipment and personnel it will need to remain in combat.

That challenge has always been daunting, but it is even more so today when — as then Gen. Wayne Eyre told Parliament in 2023 — at Ukraine War rates of expenditure, Canada would exhaust some types of battle-decisive munitions “ in days ” while replenishing them could take years. Add to that the challenge of replacing soldiers killed or wounded at Ukraine War rates, and Canada’s sustainment challenge appears overwhelming.

And finally, there’s the doctrinal problem. The Canadian Army, like many NATO armies, is proving slow to adopt tactics, organizational structures and command-and-control practices that the war in Ukraine has demonstrated are key to survival, let alone victory, in today’s battlespace. While perhaps understandable, this leaves open the possibility that, despite all the insights and promises in Inflection Point, Canada’s new army will continue to comprise hollow formations lacking the survivability, flexibility and lethality envisioned in the plan.

To an American reader, all this may sound like an Ottawa problem of little interest to Washington. But, as in the Second World War, the ability of the Canadian Army to fight and win on foreign battlefields matters enormously to Washington. American victory in some future battle might well come down to the ability of a highly-trained, appropriately organized and well-equipped Canadian unit to show up at just the right moment — as at Potenza in 1943.

Let’s hope we don’t face a re-run of Salerno anytime soon. But if we do, let’s hope the Canadian Army is well past its inflection point, and fully prepared to reprise its victory at Potenza.

Andrew Latham is a professor of international relations at Macalester College in Saint Paul, Minn., a senior fellow at the Institute for Peace and Diplomacy.

articles.title: Tracy Brabin rules out business class flight for India trip
articles.summary: West Yorkshire's mayor answers questions about a trade mission to India and early prisoner release.
articles.body:
The Mayor of West Yorkshire says she will not be flying business class when she goes to India later this month on a trade mission.

Labour's Tracy Brabin has been answering questions on Message the Mayor on BBC Radio Leeds.

She has also been talking about the early release of prisoners, the new buses being built for West Yorkshire and increasing investment in the area.

Read our takeaways from the interview below or listen to the full interview here .

Never flown business or first class on the public purse

Last month, the mayor was asked if she would be flying business or economy class on an upcoming trade mission to India.

Today, Brabin has confirmed she will not be flying business - and never has, at taxpayers' expense.

"I'm a Yorkshire woman - I know the value of things.

"But jet lag is a real thing and I want to work really hard for the people of West Yorkshire. It's breakfast meetings right through to the evenings - these are long days and intense."

Not all Weaver Network buses will be brand new

"Where the older buses don't meet our new, better standards, they'll be cascaded elsewhere.

"It's a combination of how old are they, are they not fit for purpose?

"[The new buses] have air conditioning, two spaces for wheelchairs and a buggy, you can charge your phone.

"What we want, in time, is for the whole of the network to have these new electric buses."

The first of the new Weaver Network buses have started rolling off the production line in Northern Ireland.

We need to work together to tackle rough sleeping

Brabin was asked how she is responding to the Prime Minister's call to offer all rough sleepers accommodation this winter.

"I have got extra resources and of course I'm working with local authorities - because they know their area best - and also the voluntary and community sector.

"So it's not just me - it's a community that is going to respond to this really wicked issue on our streets."

But the mayor says, as well as finding temporary accommodation, it is important to build more affordable homes so people can "rebuild their lives."

We need to drive up the money in people's pockets

The theme of last week's Labour Party conference was "hope again". Kate from Leeds asked the mayor what her "biggest hope" is for West Yorkshire.

"We have got to level up West Yorkshire in relation to the rest of the country.

"I am doing everything I can to bring in more investment and create more jobs, getting more people into colleges and increase connectivity so people can move around our region.

"If we can grow our economy, and I am hopeful that we will, then people will have more money in their pockets."

After recently being the victim of a burglary, Nicola from Keighley asked the mayor what is being done to stop criminals reoffending once they are released from jail.

"We want to make sure in West Yorkshire that we can stop that - by rehabilitating offenders and providing opportunities for them to get into work to build a decent life," says Brabin.

"My job as the Police and Crime Commissioner is also to prevent crime."

articles.title: In Gaza, we cannot even begin to recover from trauma
articles.summary: The genocide has killed many and left the rest broken. For us, survivors, recovery is not on the horizon.
articles.body:
It has been three years of the genocidal horror in Gaza. Three years of death, destruction, despair and doom.

More than 74,000 people have been killed, including more than 1,400 since the so-called “ceasefire” took effect in October last year. Countless others have died preventable deaths due to lack of healthcare.

The rest of us survivors live in permanent trauma – a trauma we can’t begin to recover from because the genocide has not stopped.

The scale of the psychological devastation is difficult to put into words. There are some numbers that international organisations have started to use to call for urgent attention to the “mental health crisis”.

Analysis by the United Nations Population Fund has concluded that more than one million children in Gaza require psychosocial support, and 96 percent of them feel that death is imminent.

Among adolescents and young adults, approximately 61 percent suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), 38 percent from depression and 41 percent from anxiety.

One study estimated that some 88 percent of adults in Gaza have PTSD.

These are children and adults who had already been traumatised by repeated wars before. By 2020 – after three months-long wars – half of Gaza’s children displayed symptoms of PTSD. By 2022, 71 percent of adults had depression.

What these numbers do not say is what it is like to live with trauma when the chance of recovery is not even on the horizon.

We had known war before, but not total genocidal war.

Nothing prepared us for it. Not running from our homes when the Israeli army invaded in 2008. Not taking cover when Israeli bombardment levelled homes in 2012, 2014 and 2021.

Total, never-ending war is different. It overpowers; it crushes because it eliminates the hope of survival.

I had read about it in books. Hemingway’s A Farewell to Arms comes to mind.

I remember the detailed descriptions of shelling and gunfire, of mangled limbs, dead bodies carried away on stretchers, doctors covered in blood like “butchers”.

Death in Gaza is nothing like that. It has a smell: of gunpowder, of burning rubble, of something rotten. It has a sound: a whoosh of a missile and the muffled screams from under the rubble. It has a bodily feeling of pure terror.

Nothing in the war prose I read prepared me for what I have seen and experienced.

In the first two months of the war, six houses in my immediate neighbourhood were bombed, and 60 of my neighbours were killed. One bomb fell so close that it burst a wall and windows of our house, injuring my younger sister, my mother and me.

The bombing was incessant – day and night. During the day, the smoke would fill up the air and hide the blue of the sky. At night, the dark and dust would be pierced by phone torches, as we would rush to dig our neighbours out of the rubble.

I saw a child’s body lodged in a shattered wall next to a man’s severed hand.

I lifted the corpse of a baby from under the ruins.

I watched a mother get out from under a collapsed home, blood streaming down her cheeks, while smoke-filled faces screamed and terror-stricken neighbours rummaged through pulverised concrete walls looking for their families.

And one horrific day, I found my own eight-year-old student Mohammed face down in the rubble. I rolled him onto his back to check for a pulse. No pulse, no breath. He had been coming to my house for English lessons with his sister. The bombing took his innocent life, but spared his sister. I pulled her out alive.

My trauma is stuck in my body like shrapnel. It tightens my chest when a drone passes overhead. It shakes my hands when I hear the crack of gunfire nearby.

I feel numb. I cannot concentrate. I almost never smile.

“The world breaks everyone and afterward many are strong at the broken places. But those that will not break it kills. It kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially,” Hemingway wrote.

Indeed, it is not just the trauma that has overcome us, the broken people. It is also the survivor’s guilt. The very best and the most noble have been taken away from us. I have lost relatives, friends, students: the brightest, the most generous, the kindest.

I no longer read to learn and enrich myself. I read to forget. I read until my vision gets blurry and sleep overcomes me, as I try to keep images of death out of my head.

Fiction can no longer move me, shock me. I saw humanity die and the rest of the world watch on, indifferently. What could be more fictional than this?

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: ‘Not the act of a friend’: Israel’s deadline to close UK consulate nears
articles.summary: Former British consul Sir Vincent Fean says Israel is acting unlawfully in the wake of a new wave of sanctions.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – The deadline Israel imposed on the United Kingdom to close its East Jerusalem consulate is fast approaching.

Thursday marks 30 days since Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar’s order, a retaliatory move against the UK’s wave of sanctions targeting illegal Israeli settlements.

“It’s not the act of a friend or ally,” Sir Vincent Fean, former British consul general to Jerusalem, told Al Jazeera. “The British Consulate General has every right to be in Jerusalem, in East Jerusalem, part of the state of Palestine.”

From 2010 until 2014, Fean held the post as the de facto ambassador to occupied Palestinian territory. He is now a trustee of the Britain Palestine Project, advocating for equal rights for Palestinians and Israelis.

“In international law, for [the UK], and for the vast majority of the world, Israel does not have the right to interfere with the diplomatic relations between the state of Palestine and the state of the United Kingdom. It is doing so by closing our office, and that is unlawful,” he said, adding that he is “particularly concerned” for the consulate’s 50 or so Palestinian staff.

UK-Israel ties have reached a nadir. On Monday, reports claimed that the UK could expel 27 Israeli diplomats if the consulate closure goes ahead.

British National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell has reportedly held talks with Israeli officials in a visit that was not disclosed by the UK government, but an agreement to keep the consulate open was not reached.

Israel’s response was furious following the UK’s import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, as well as an overall change of tone. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has, for instance, lamented Israel’s “ethnic cleansing” against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband expected Israel to retaliate, but said the UK had “weighed the costs and benefits of acting”.

In addition to the consulate closure order, Israel expelled the UK from the Washington-led coordination centre for post-war Gaza and barred 11 lawmakers from entering Israel, including former Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana.

“It is illegal and unlawful for Israel to act in this way,” Fean told Al Jazeera. “There’s been a reset in UK foreign policy since [Prime Minister Andy] Burnham and Miliband came in.”

Israel’s hostile actions towards the UK “will not be forgiven or forgotten anytime soon”, he added.

In a brief by the Britain Palestine Project that was endorsed by former UK Attorney General Dominic Grieve KC and shared with Al Jazeera, the threatened closure is described as “an unlawful assertion of sovereignty over occupied Palestinian territory”.

“The Israeli announcement usurps the rights of the State of Palestine,” it reads.

Resolution 478 was adopted by the United Nations Security Council – of which the UK is a permanent member – in 1980, resolving that Israel’s attempts to alter the status of Jerusalem are “null and void”.

In 2016, Resolution 2334 reiterated this, “condemning all measures aimed at altering the demographic composition, character and status of the Palestinian Territory occupied since 1967, including East Jerusalem”.

The UK formally recognised the State of Palestine in September of 2025 .

If the UK resists Israel’s orders, there are various logistical challenges Israel could feasibly impose on the consulate and the diplomats within it.

“The practicality is that the Consulate General depends on Israeli electricity [and] water. So there are means by which Israel could force the expulsion, the closure, of the Consulate General,” Fean told Al Jazeera. “I don’t know what’s going to happen, but this Israeli government has broken many laws,” he said when asked if Israel may use electricity or water cut-offs as a means to expel British diplomats.

While reiterating that the UK’s East Jerusalem consulate should remain open despite orders, Fean said that “if that proves to be made impossible by force of the Israeli government, then there are alternatives.”

Foreign embassies in Ramallah could be an alternate route to manage consulate affairs, he said.

The consulate acts as the channel of communications between the UK and the Palestinian government and manages consular affairs for British nationals in the region, including pilgrims to the West Bank.

“Yet again, Israel is taking it out on the Palestinians for something that somebody else has done,” said Fean. “The impunity of Israel needs to be challenged. The fact that this Israeli government seems to see itself as above the law needs to be challenged.”

Human rights advocates have urged the UK to resist Israel’s orders.

“Such a retaliatory step from Israel suggests that any further measures taken by the UK could trigger further responses,” said Zena Agha, deputy director of the British Palestinian Committee. “But that should not deter the UK from meeting its obligations under international law – nor pursuing measures towards accountability for Israel’s genocide and occupation.”

Shamiul Joarder, director of Friends of al-Aqsa, reiterated the illegality of Israel’s actions and told Al Jazeera, “If Britain accepts this order, it risks allowing Israel to dictate the terms of Britain’s diplomatic presence in occupied East Jerusalem. That would set a deeply concerning precedent.”

The Foreign, Commonwealth, and Development Office (FCDO) did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on Israel’s orders to close the British Consulate, nor on the UK’s intended response.

articles.title: Rubio calls on Russia to provide more information about plague lab death
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday called on Russia to provide more information surrounding a suspected pneumonic plague outbreak in the country after a woman working at a laboratory handling the deadly pathogens died. While the World Health Organization said Tuesday the risk of spread in Russia and to Europe is generally low, it…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday called on Russia to provide more information surrounding a suspected pneumonic plague outbreak in the country after a woman working at a laboratory handling the deadly pathogens died.

While the World Health Organization said Tuesday the risk of spread in Russia and to Europe is generally low, it is waiting for an official assessment from the Russian Federation.

Rubio, speaking to reporters while on diplomatic travel in Iceland, said it is “incumbent” on Russia to share more information with the world.

“We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world so that all of us could react accordingly and appropriately,” he said.

Rubio’s remarks come less than a week after Russian media reports highlighted the death of a woman who worked at a laboratory in Russia’s Irkutsk oblast, with authorities looking into whether she was infected with pneumonic plague.

Her workplace studies dangerous pathogens, including plague, in a part of Siberia where plague occurs naturally in wild animals, the WHO said in a statement provided to The Hill’s partner, NewsNation.

Pneumonic plague is a rare but often fatal disease that can be transmitted by respiratory droplets from animals or persons infected with the Yersinia pestis bacteria, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention .

Nearly 200 people are under observation of possible infection, related to possible contact with the deceased woman, according to reports , including more than 100 in hospital wards.
